# How sure are you? {#could-be}

## The gap {#gap}

English *I think* often introduces a guess, and a painful guess introduced that way is easily mistaken for a fact. *Probably*, *maybe*, and *definitely* are vague, and two people can interpret the same one very differently. Ageben has one word for *could be*, and its ending says what you plan to do about your guess.

## The forms {#forms}
<!-- Agent summary: three drop-ins for could be (table): says it could be so, not that it is, and gives no reason. Ending = what you'll do about the guess: `thomal` find out, `thomam` (default) unsaid, `thomar` not followed up. Placement: where English puts *probably*; covers its clause. Unsure → `thomam`. Omit when you mean it is so. Most useful on painful guesses. -->

Each drop-in marks a sentence as a guess. It says that something *could be* so, without claiming that it is, and it gives no reason for the guess.

The three differ only in their last letter, which says what you will do about the guess: find out, say nothing about a next step, or not follow it up.

| Drop-in | Meaning | What you'll do about the guess |
|---------|---------|--------------------------------|
| `thomal` | could be, and I'll find out | find out |
| `thomam` | could be (the default) | say nothing about it |
| `thomar` | could be, who knows | not follow it up |

Put the drop-in where English would put *probably*: at the end of the clause, at the start, or next to the word you are unsure of. Wherever it goes, it applies to the whole clause it sits in. When you can't tell which ending fits, use `thomam`, which says *could be* and nothing about a next step.

Use the drop-in most on painful guesses, such as a rejection, a loss, or a friend who seems upset with you. These are the guesses most often said with *I think* and then believed as facts. When you mean that something is so, leave the drop-in out.

## What the ending says {#endings}
<!-- Agent summary: ending = follow-up on the guess: `-l` you will find out, `-m` (default) unsaid, `-r` a passing thought you're not pursuing right now. None is better. This is the settled-to-passing scale: `-l` most settled (≈ lasting), `-m` default, `-r` most passing (≈ right now). It recurs on other drop-ins; each word gives the three endings its own meaning, same direction. -->

The last letter of the drop-in is its ending. On this word, the ending says whether you will follow up on the guess. For example, here is the same worry with each ending:

> She's upset with me `thomal`.  
> She's upset with me `thomam`.  
> She's upset with me `thomar`.

With `thomal`, you will find out, for example by asking her tonight. With `thomam`, you say it could be and say nothing about a next step. With `thomar`, it is a passing thought: you considered it and will not follow it up now.

No ending is better than the others. Checking, leaving a guess at *could be*, and not following it up are all reasonable, so choose the ending that matches what you will do.

The same three endings, `-l`, `-m`, and `-r`, appear on many other drop-ins. Together they form the **settled-to-passing scale**, which runs from most settled to most passing. `-l` is the settled end, and on this word it means the question will be settled. `-m` is the middle and the default. `-r` is the passing end, and on this word it means a thought that applies only to right now.

Each drop-in gives the three endings its own meaning, but the direction is always the same, and later lessons rely on it. Think of `-l` as *lasting* and `-r` as *right now*. When a later drop-in takes an ending, ask what lasting and right now mean for that word.

## Examples {#examples}

> The package arrives Friday `thomam`.  
> My application got rejected `thomam`.  
> It'll rain `thomar`.  
> I left the stove on `thomal`.  
> The flight's delayed `thomam`.

*I left the stove on `thomal`* says you might have, and you will go back to check. *It'll rain `thomar`* is a passing thought, so you will not check the forecast. *My application got rejected `thomam`* says the rejection is possible, not that you have been told.

## Telling a guess apart {#telling-apart}
<!-- Agent summary: near misses. No drop-in = saying it is so; a later plain sentence settles the guess and doesn't contradict it. *I think* reporting the act of thinking (*I'm thinking about the trip*) is no guess and stays plain English. Claims only: on a command or request the drop-in has no reading. -->

Three other things are easily confused with a guess, and each is handled differently.

### A guess or a fact {#guess-or-fact}

Without the drop-in, a sentence says that something is so. *The flight's delayed* states it as a fact, and *the flight's delayed `thomam`* says only that it could be. So when you have seen the departures board yourself, leave the drop-in out.

A later plain sentence does not contradict the guess. Suppose you said *I left the stove on `thomal`* and then found the stove off. Saying *the stove is off* settles the question. It does not make the earlier sentence wrong, because that sentence never claimed the stove was on.

### A guess or a thought {#guess-or-thought}

When *I think* describes an activity, as in *I'm thinking about the trip*, it is not a guess, and it stays in plain English. The drop-in is for the other *I think*, the one in *I think she's upset with me*. To tell the two apart, replace *I think* with *could be*: if the meaning stays the same, the sentence is a guess.

### A claim or a request {#claim-or-request}

The drop-in goes on a claim, a sentence that says how things are or could be. A request or an order is not a claim, so the drop-in has nothing to mark in it. For example, *close the window `thomam`* is not a softer request. It has no meaning, so leave the drop-in off and ask in plain English.

## Saying the words {#saying}
<!-- Agent summary: pronunciation keywords (table). Each letter one sound, always the same; each vowel its own beat (`thomam` = two beats); two vowel letters = two beats. Light stress on the first beat; vowels stay full, never *uh*. -->

Every drop-in in this course is a real Ageben word, so pronounce it as Ageben does. Each letter has one sound, the same every time, and each vowel is its own beat. So `thomam` has two beats, one for each vowel, and two vowel letters in a row are also two beats.

| Letter | Sounds like |
|--------|-------------|
| `a` | *spa* |
| `e` | *bet* |
| `o` | *no*, without the glide |
| `u` | *you*, without the *y* |
| `th` | the sound in *this* |

Stress the first beat lightly, saying it slightly louder than the rest. Pronounce the other vowels fully as well. English reduces unstressed vowels to *uh*, like the second *a* in *banana*, but an Ageben vowel keeps its sound at any speed.

## Practice {#practice}

Add the drop-in that fits the note.

**1.** *The store is closed.* (could be; you'll call and check)

::: details Show answer
The store is closed `thomal`.
:::

**2.** *The store is closed.* (could be; that's all you're saying)

::: details Show answer
The store is closed `thomam`.
:::

**3.** *The store is closed.* (could be; you won't look into it)

::: details Show answer
The store is closed `thomar`.
:::

**4.** *He forgot.* (could be; you aren't saying more)

::: details Show answer
He forgot `thomam`.
:::

**5.** *He forgot.* (could be, and you'll ask him tomorrow)

::: details Show answer
He forgot `thomal`.
:::

**6.** *Aliens built it.* (a passing thought)

::: details Show answer
Aliens built it `thomar`.
:::
